Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Ebola DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever Rachel Savage and agencies Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.17 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago. The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa , the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data. Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak. The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace. Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported. Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded. The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real. Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say Read more Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months. The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February. Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate. Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.” Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”. Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months. Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal. Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time. This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola. Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate. Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story. https://english.radio.cz/coalition-lawma.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Coalition lawmakers seek to remove statute of limitations for premeditated murder Facebook Twitter A group of coalition lawmakers from ANO, Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) and the Motorists party has proposed abolishing the statute of limitations for premeditated murder and several other intentional homicide offences. The amendment would also apply to selected crimes related to public endangerment, terrorism and terror offences carrying the possibility of exceptional sentences. It was submitted as part of a broader amendment expanding criminal liability for failure to pay child support. Under current Czech law, murder cases are subject to a 30-year statute of limitations, after which criminal liability expires. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/world/presi.text: The Budapest Times President calls out UN’s double standards at General Assembly The United Nations is in a crisis of trust and too often remains inactive when major powers and their allies break the rules, András Baka, the President of the Republic, declared on Thursday in New York, in a speech delivered at the high-level session of the UN General Assembly. Speaking on behalf of Hungary, the head of state stressed that no country can stand above the law, and that allies cannot be held to a different standard than other countries. However, this does not mean that the UN should be turned away from. “We need it, and we need it to work,” said András Baka. He added that the UN must be capable of action, must treat all member states fairly, and must apply the same principles to everyone. Speaking about Hungary, András Baka warned that a new political majority must not be allowed to become the new owner of the state. People want the rule of law, he said — they want the state to serve rather than control everything, for courts to make their decisions free from pressure, and for the press to hold power to account. According to him, corruption and abuse of power must be followed by accountability, but this cannot amount to revenge, and justice must not become a political weapon. The same laws must apply to those who governed in the past, those who govern today, and those who may govern in the future, he pointed out. “A republic begins when power accepts its limits. It is this republic that Hungary must now rebuild” — the head of state stated. In his speech, he pointed out that the trust of Hungary’s partners will not return as a result of a single election or a single speech, and therefore called for the country to be judged by its actions. Hungary will be a reliable member of the European Union, a committed ally of NATO, and an active member of the United Nations, he stressed. Recalling the 1956 revolution, he said that the uprising expressed the Hungarian people’s determination to decide their own fate, but that this hope was crushed by Soviet tanks. The calls of the Hungarian people reached the United Nations, but the international community was unable to prevent the suppression of the revolution. “Today, Ukraine is fighting to preserve its independence” — he stressed, recalling that Hungary condemns Russia’s full-scale war of aggression and stands by Ukraine’s right to self-defence, its sovereignty, and its territorial integrity. “The freedom for which Hungarians fought in 1956 is the freedom we must defend for Ukrainians today” — he declared. As he stated, Hungary would like to see the fighting brought to an end through diplomatic means, but lasting peace requires respect for Ukraine’s sovereignty. “If violent territorial seizure becomes an accepted way of settling disputes, every smaller country will have reason to fear for its future,” he warned. Turning to the Middle East, András Baka called for full respect for international humanitarian law and the safe, unimpeded delivery of aid. He stressed that Israelis and Palestinians must be able to live in safety and dignity. Any lasting peace must create a future in which children can grow up without fear. On the topic of migration, he stressed that every state has the right to protect its borders. He added that Hungary would act in accordance with international law to combat illegal migration and the criminal organisations profiting from it, while respecting human dignity and the protections owed to refugees. Closing his speech, he noted that trust in the United Nations cannot be demanded — it can only be earned — and that the same applies to every state and public institution. Trust in the future must be restored in Hungary, and the country must become one that others can rely on. Artificial intelligence was used for the translation of parts of the original Hungarian text. https://www.dw.com/en/trump-putin-agree-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O5fo Trump said he had had a 'highly successful' discussion with Putin [FILE: August 15, 2025] Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release Russian diesel to US and global markets. The move, which aims to address rising fuel costs before the US midterm elections, marks a dramatic turnaround in US policy toward Moscow since the start of the war in Ukraine . In a social media post, Trump wrote he had made a deal with Putin during a phone call that was supposed to be about a suspected plague outbreak in Russia . What did Trump say? According to Trump, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Trump wrote that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that. The US Treasury Department issued a temporary license that will allow Russian diesel to reach global markets through April 2027. Trump's announcement follows his signing of a broad Russia sanctions law last month. The law is intended to clamp down on Russia’s energy sector and other areas that fuel its war against Ukraine. Trump under growing pressure at home to address rising fuel costs Image: David Dee Delgado/REUTERS What did Russian officials say? Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian presidential envoy, reposted the Treasury Department's announcement on X, saying that "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world." Alexander Novak, Russia's Deputy Prime Minister, said that the country was ready to start supplying additional volumes of diesel to the United States and other countries from October. He also said that Russia's exports are expected to rise further in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance. Later, the Kremlin released a statement from Putin saying that, during their call, he and Trump had also devoted "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and had discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations." How has Ukraine reacted? Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has condemned the agreement, saying that any easing of sanctions without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of "weakness." "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," he wrote on social media. "Allowing Russia to ⁠sell ​petroleum products ​is an investment in a ​war that ‌must be ended, not prolonged. What ​is needed ⁠is real de-escalation with Russia ⁠on ​a reciprocal basis," the Ukrainian president stressed. Zelenskyy added that Ukraine hopes the US will have a strong conversation with Russia: "A strong one, not a weak one." Sanctions against Russia Since its 2022 full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine, Moscow has been hit with waves of sanctions by the United States and its Western partners. But as the war has continued with no resolution in sight, Washington's commitment has appeared to waver. Earlier this year, temporary US sanctions waivers that allowed the sale of Russian oil raised concerns because they could hinder efforts to deprive Moscow of funds for its war in Ukraine. Last month, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring diesel prices, and even publicly told Zelenskyy to stop the attacks. Trump's announcement on Friday came just as US, Ukrainian, and European officials were meeting in Miami for new diplomatic talks aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine. According to US envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian, European, US and NATO representatives held constructive discussions in Miami, and agreed to continue diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What's behind Trump's deal with Putin? According to Ines Pohl, the chief of DW's Washington D.C. bureau, the diesel deal is mainly about domestic politics. With the midterms only weeks away, Trump is under heavy pressure over high energy prices . The deal allows him to show that he is taking action and appeal to voters who feel the rising cost of fuel directly, while the war in Ukraine seems far away. Politically, that is significant: Trump is accepting a loosening of sanctions on Russia, even though Washington had actually wanted to increase pressure on Putin. It also makes one thing crystal clear: when push comes to shove, Trump consistently chooses what benefits him personally over what Congress has decided . He appears to be betting that, for many Americans, prices at the pump matter more in the end than the geopolitical consequences. Whether the promised deliveries will actually bring noticeable relief, however, remains doubtful. War abroad, soaring prices at home: is Trump in trouble? https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: Ukraine struck an oil terminal in St. Petersburg Sunday morning in what Russian state media called “one of the biggest drone attacks of the year.” Alexander Beglov, governor of St. Petersburg, said on Telegram Sunday that the city underwent a “massive” overnight attack from Ukrainian drones. “The Ministry of Emergency Situations continues to extinguish fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district,” he said, adding that one person died and several others were injured in the incident. The drone strikes come as Kyiv and Moscow ramp up attacks on each other’s infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week he had ordered the resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries following a three-day pause after U.S. President Donald Trump declared he had brokered an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. Advertisement Advertisement Trump repeatedly urged Ukraine to halt its attacks and blamed the country for rising fuel prices — while also calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as president . Writing on X Sunday morning, the Ukrainian president highlighted Moscow’s continued attacks on Ukraine. “In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic,” he wrote, adding that the U.S. “should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements.” Separately, Vilnius said that a suspected drone may have self-detonated in Lithuania while on a flight path toward Latvia Sunday morning. A spokesperson for the Lithuanian armed forces said NATO air defense mission fighter jets were scrambled in response to the incident near the Latvian border. The provenance of the suspected drone is unclear, but Robertas ​Kaunas, Lithuania’s defense minister, said the object was likely a ​drone which had entered the country from Poland, adding that he had proposed a ⁠joint investigation with his Polish counterpart. Police searches are also underway in eastern Poland after reports of an unidentified object entering the country’s airspace following a Russian attack on Ukraine.
